title: Canada Airports Launch Free Flow Transit, Letting International Passengers Skip Border Checks
excerpt: Toronto Pearson, Vancouver, and Montréal-Trudeau now let connecting international travelers bypass customs entirely, saving up to 60 minutes on layovers.
body:
• Canada's Free Flow International-to-International Transit process, launched June 26, lets connecting passengers skip in-person border checks at Toronto Pearson, Vancouver, and Montréal-Trudeau airports.
  • Airlines now share passenger data electronically with the Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA), replacing the old kiosk-based check-in system and saving travelers 30 to 60 minutes.
  • Passengers must connect within 24 hours, have through-checked baggage, and carry valid travel documents — US-bound travelers still clear CBP Preclearance.
  • Calgary, Edmonton, and Halifax have signalled interest in joining the program, which other airports can adopt by applying to CBSA.

Canada has become the first country to eliminate compulsory border screening for international-to-international transit passengers, launching a Free Flow program that lets connecting travelers skip customs and proceed directly to their departure gate at the country's three busiest airports.

The Canada Border Services Agency (CBSA) rolled out the Free Flow International-to-International Transit process on June 26, 2026, at Toronto Pearson International Airport (Terminal 1), Vancouver International Airport, and Montréal-Trudeau International Airport — hubs that handled a combined 49.3 million international travelers last year.

How the New System Works

Under the previous system, international transit passengers were required to stop at a CBSA kiosk and check in with border services, even if they had no intention of entering Canada. That requirement is now gone.

Instead, airlines collect and transmit passenger flight details — including final destination and scheduled departure time — directly to CBSA. The agency performs advance risk screening behind the scenes using an Advance Passenger Information and Passenger Name Record (API-PNR) model, similar to the system used at major U.S. hubs.

"The Free Flow International-to-International Transit process is one of the ways the CBSA is improving the traveller experience while maintaining the security of Canada's border," said Rob Chambers, Vice President of CBSA's Travellers Branch. "We are working with our airport partners to provide a simpler and more efficient process for travellers to get to their international destinations without delay."

"The CBSA is putting in place tools and technologies, and updating processes to build the border of the future."

— Rob Chambers, VP Travellers Branch, Canada Border Services Agency

Eligibility and Fine Print

The program applies to passengers who meet specific criteria. Travelers must connect from one international flight to another within 24 hours of arrival, stay within the airport's international transit or departure area, have through-checked baggage to their final destination, and travel on a single-ticket itinerary. Valid travel documents — including a Canadian airport transit visa or Electronic Travel Authorization (eTA) where applicable — remain mandatory.

Critically, the exemption does not extend to U.S.-bound passengers. Anyone whose final destination is the United States must still complete U.S. immigration and customs through Customs and Border Protection (CBP) Preclearance at the Canadian airport before boarding their connecting flight.

The Free Flow corridor also ends if a layover exceeds 24 hours, baggage is not interlined, or the passenger leaves the sterile international area — any of these triggers full border processing.

What It Means for Indian Travelers

The policy shift is particularly relevant for Indian travelers, who frequently route flights through Canadian airports. Air India operates direct flights from New Delhi and Mumbai to Toronto, with onward connections to U.S. destinations through codeshare and interline partners including WestJet. The new system eliminates an unpredictable bottleneck that previously forced some passengers to book flexible fares or overnight layovers to protect against missed connections.

For NRIs traveling between India and the United States via Canada, the time savings could be substantial. According to the Canadian Global Mobility Association, roughly 18 percent of corporate trips routed through Canada involve same-day onward flights. The program eliminates the kiosk check-in step that could add 30 to 60 minutes to connection times.

Expansion Plans

The three launch airports are not the end of the road. CBSA has opened the program to other airports, which can apply to adopt the Free Flow process. Calgary, Edmonton, and Halifax have already signalled interest, though CBSA officials noted that adoption requires significant IT integration and secure-zone modifications.

The regulatory framework was published in the Canada Gazette for a 30-day consultation period before implementation, and CBSA says the system was successfully tested at all three launch airports before going live.
nri_angle: Indian travelers routing through Canadian airports to the US will benefit from faster connections, especially on the popular Delhi/Mumbai-Toronto-US corridor.
